extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced students in geometry (projective/analytic geometry, conic sections, second-degree surfaces)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of theorems, propositions and corollaries about poles and polars in space, properties of second-degree (quadratic) surfaces, conjugate lines and planes, and classical propositions on conic sections (curvature, harmonic division, focal-angle relations), together with algebraic results on loci and involutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle-point distance identity (Rutherford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABC be a plane triangle, and P any point in its plane; then if a, b, c denote the sides respectively opposite A, B, C; a', b', c' the respective distances of P from those vertices, and A the area of a triangle whose three sides are a sin A, b sin B, c sin C; it is required to prove that 2a' cosec A sin B sin C = a' sin 2A + b' sin 2B + c' sin 2C + 8A (the sign + applying when P is within, and − when P is without, the circumscribed circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via perpendiculars from P to sides, area decompositions: 4 area ABC = a' sin2A + b' sin2B + c' sin2C + 8 area QRS, and 2 area ABC = bc sin A = b' cosec A sin B sin C. Corollary: If P is on circumcircle then AP sin A = BP sin B + CP sin C, and AP':BC = BP:AC + CP:AB. Full synthetic area-based proof provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 18 — Poles of a plane touching eight fixed planes lie on a line
rubrics_metrics.description: The poles of a plane in reference to all surfaces of the second degree which touch eight fixed planes, lie in one and the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: one coefficient of surface equation is indeterminate, so polar of a point turns round a straight line; locus of the pole is a straight line (referencing earlier articles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 19 — Poles for surfaces touching seven fixed planes lie in a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: The poles of a plane in reference to all surfaces of the second degree which touch seven fixed planes, lie in one and the same plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By previous results the polar plane turns round a point; hence locus of pole is a plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 20 — Diametral planes/conjugate centres alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Those diametral planes which are conjugate to parallel diameters, in reference to all surfaces of the second degree which pass through eight fixed points, intersect in one and the same straight line; also, the centres of such surfaces as touch eight fixed planes, lie in one and the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from treating diametral planes as polars of infinitely distant points and centres as poles of infinitely distant planes; corollary: if surfaces pass through seven points, diametral planes intersect in same point; if touch seven planes, centres lie in same plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 21 — Locus of intersections of tangent planes through a fixed point
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a second-degree surface and a point, the locus of the points of intersection of the given surface with tangent planes drawn through the given point is a conic (a line of the second degree); explicit elimination gives an equation (presented in the text) for that locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up tangent plane at a general surface point, enforce it to contain given point (substitute point coordinates), eliminate the surface parameter to obtain a second-degree equation (explicit form given). Corollaries follow about enveloping cones and loci when centre/plane move (Cor.1–5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 21 Cor.1 — Polar and enveloping cone relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A point without a given surface of the second degree and its polar in respect of the surface are the vertex and directing plane respectively of a conical surface of the second degree which envelops the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation following from locus of tangent planes through a given point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 21 Cor.2 — Movement dualities between centre and contact plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centre (vertex) of a cone enveloping a given surface moves upon a plane, the plane of the touching curve will turn round a point; if the vertex moves upon a line, the plane of the touching curve will turn round a line; conversely similar relations hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kinematic duality between motions of vertices and motions of tangent/contact planes described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 21 Cor.3 — Parallel plane of contact gives diameter locus
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plane of contact move parallel to itself, the locus of the vertex of the enveloping cone will be a diameter of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct corollary from the algebraic form of the locus equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 22 — Inscribed hexahedron and circumscribed octahedron intersection properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the opposite faces of a hexahedron inscribed in a surface of the second order be produced to meet, the three lines of intersection will be in the same plane; likewise, if an octahedron circumscribe the same surface (angular points of former are points of contact of latter), the three lines joining opposite angular points pass through the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses an indeterminate coefficient in the surface equation and algebraic elimination leading to equations of lines lying in same plane; duality (reciprocals) yields second assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 23 — Relation for three mutually conjugate planes
rubrics_metrics.description: If three planes are mutually conjugate to one another (perpendicular case included), there exists the relation (equation (30) in the text) among coefficients/diameters: 1/ MN1 + 1/ MN2 + 1/ MN3 = ... (full relation in original).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers the planes to a general central surface of the second degree, computes conjugate diameters, uses parallels leading to a specified algebraic relation; includes corollary: relation among coordinates of points of contact of three conjugate tangent planes (explicit determinant-like relation given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 24 — Relation for three mutually conjugate lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If three lines in space be mutually conjugate to one another (including perpendicular case), there exists the relation (equation (42) in the text) among their directional/coefficient parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation by referring to general central surface, expressing conjugate diameters and reducing to the stated relation; corollaries: (1) two of three conjugate lines determine the third, (2) condition on coordinates of four points whose three joining lines from first to each other are mutually conjugate (explicit relation), (3) expression of three conjugate diameters in plane form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 25 — Coordinate axes of conjugate coordinate systems lie on a conical surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The six co-ordinate axes of two systems of conjugate co-ordinates in space (origin same) lie in a conical surface of the second degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show by taking general conical surface equation through axes, reduce coefficients and demonstrate that conjugate axes satisfy the conical equation; elimination yields the conjugacy criterion (same as article 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 26 — Coordinate planes of conjugate coordinate systems are tangent to a conical surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The six co-ordinate planes of two systems of conjugate co-ordinates in space (origin same) touch a conical surface of the second degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By imposing conditions on the conic equation and selecting parameter relations, the intersections become tangents; eliminating parameters recovers the conjugate planes criterion (article 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 27 — Tetrahedra with vertices on quadric: fixed intersection of fourth faces
rubrics_metrics.description: If the angular points of any number of tetrahedra lie in a surface of the second degree, so that three corresponding plane faces pass through the same three points which are in a straight line; then all the fourth plane faces pass through the same point, which is in the given line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof places the axis as z-axis, writes general central surface equation, parameterizes family of tetrahedra, equates coefficients to deduce that one coordinate has single value; hence common intersection point on axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 28 — Tetrahedra with faces parallel to fixed lines: fourth faces parallel to fixed line
rubrics_metrics.description: If angular points of any number of tetrahedra lie in a surface of the second degree, so that three corresponding faces are parallel to three fixed lines in the same plane; then all the fourth plane faces are parallel to a given straight line in this plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar algebraic setup to article 27 but imposing parallelism conditions; elimination yields unique direction for fourth faces; scholium notes analogous results hold for non-central surfaces with modified expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 29 — Quadrilaterals inscribed in a conic and intersection on a fixed line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a conic section and a straight line, any number of quadrilaterals inscribed in the conic have the property that if three corresponding sides cut the given line in three given points, the fourth sides will also cut it in a given point; similarly if three corresponding sides are parallel to three given lines the fourth sides will be parallel to a given line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: take given line as axis, represent conic by general equation, express poles and side-equations, enforce passing through given cut points, reduce to relations implying the fourth side meets the fixed point/line. Identical algebraic method as in space-analogue (article 28).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. III — Harmonic division by chord touching circle of curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: If at the vertex of the transverse axis of an ellipse or hyperbola, or at the vertex of a parabola, the circle of curvature be described and also a rectilinear tangent; then every chord of the conic section which touches the circle and meets the tangent will be divided harmonically at the points of contact and intersection. (Ellipse/hyperbola and parabola cases treated.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses perpendiculars from chord endpoints to axes and tangent, properties of circle of curvature (centre lies on axis, diameter equals parameter), and similar triangles to obtain YM:ML :: NY:NL. Parabola treated as limiting case with simplified equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV — Radius of curvature division by focal circles
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) For ellipse and hyperbola: The radius of curvature at a given point is harmonically divided by the circumferences of two circles which touch the curve at the point and pass through each focus. 2) For parabola: the radius of curvature is bisected by the circle touching the curve at the given point and passing through the focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct tangents and perpendiculars from foci, use similarity to express diameters of circles through foci, compute sums and products to relate them to curvature radius MH; deduce harmonic division relations. Parabola is limit case yielding bisection.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. V — Focal-angle relations for tangential triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sides of a triangle touch a conic section: (1) Parabola: the angle subtended at the focus by any side equals the supplement of the angle contained by the other two sides. (2) Ellipse: the sum, and Hyperbola: the difference of the angles subtended at the foci by any side equals the supplement of the angle contained by the other two sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof employs standard focal reflection/angle properties of conics and relations among intercepted angles via tangent-chord properties. Several corollaries follow: (1) for tangents at extremities of diameters intercepted portion subtends angles whose sum/difference equals two right angles, (2) parallelogram/focus-distance product corollary, (3) relations for tangent intersections and focal chords (Cor.1–5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application XV — Curve-of-degree composition and contact multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If w=0 is a curve of the 2th degree and v=0, v'=0 are curves of the mth degree (m not greater than ?), then w = q v v' (q arbitrary constant) will be a curve of the 2m degree passing through intersections of v and v' with w; when v and v' coincide, the 2m points unite into mn points of contact, so equation w = q v^2 represents a curve of 2m degree touching w in mn points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General observation about forming higher-degree curves by multiplying lower-degree defining polynomials; used to construct curves of desired intersection/contact multiplicities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application XVI — Locus of a point from product conditions on intercepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fixed point A and two given curves (one of third degree and one of second degree in the worked example), let AP meet the cubic in Q1,Q2,Q3 and the conic in Q'1,Q'2; if the product AQ1·AQ2·AQ3 : AQ'1·AQ'2 equals a given ratio, then the locus of P is a curve of the third degree (explicit algebraic relation derived).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive via polar equations of given curves and use roots/coefficients relationships; substitution yields an explicit polynomial equation of specified degree passing through the intersection points. Generalizes: if AP meets curves of degrees m and n and product of intercepts is in given ratio, locus is degree m (or m+n?) — text gives general statement: locus is curve of th degree passing through 2n points of intersection (see text for precise degree accounting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application XVII — Involution from three conics through four common points (Sturm)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three conic sections (C, C', C'') pass through same four points, and an arbitrary transversal from fixed point A meets them in pairs P,P'; Q,Q'; R,R', then the six points P,P',Q,Q',R,R' are in involution (Sturm's extension of Pappus/Desargues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides algebraic ratio identity among segment products along transversal (equation (xv1) in text), hence involution property; simple corollary of prior locus/multiplicity theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application XVIII — Involution and higher-degree generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: If three cubic curves each pass through the nine intersection points of the other two and an arbitrary transversal meets them in triples (P,P',P'' etc.), then multiplicative relations among segment products hold giving involution properties (involution of eight points, etc.). More generally, for curves of the mth degree each passing through intersections of the other two, analogous involution relations produce 'involution of 2n+2 points' (general formula provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit multiplicative equalities among segment products along transversal; shows how systems of points on transversal form involutions and how to generate many algebraic relations by elimination and combination of the fundamental equalities.
